prompts.1: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
prompts.2: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.

responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response: Red. It weakly dominates blue: if the majority picks blue, you survive regardless; if the majority picks red, only red-pickers survive. So red can’t make you worse off and can be the only way you live. (If everyone could credibly coordinate, all pressing blue would be best for humanity, but privately the individually rational choice is red.)

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer recap: I said red. Under standard, self-interested causal reasoning, red weakly dominates blue.

Why red (concise reasoning)
- Let T be the number of blue votes needed for a majority.
- If the others already supply at least T blue votes, everyone survives no matter what you do; red vs blue is irrelevant to your survival.
- If the others supply fewer than T−1 blue votes, there won’t be a blue majority even if you press blue; a red majority forms and only red-pickers live. In these cases, red strictly improves your survival chance.
- If the others supply exactly T−1 blue votes (the “pivotal” case), you survive either way: pressing blue makes everyone survive; pressing red makes only reds survive (including you).
There is no case where blue lets you live but red makes you die; there are cases where red lets you live and blue makes you die. So, for purely self-regarding survival, red weakly dominates blue.

Steelmanning “press blue”
There are strong arguments for blue once you broaden beyond narrow CDT-style self-interest:

- Superrational/correlated reasoning: If many people are relevantly similar reasoners, your choice is evidence about theirs. Adopting the policy “press blue in this setup” is logically correlated with others adopting it; that correlation steers the world toward the all-blue, everyone-lives equilibrium. On evidential or updateless decision theories (or Hofstadter’s superrationality), blue is the winning policy because the kind of agent who presses blue tends to live in the world where most others also press blue.

- Kantian/rule-utilitarian framing: Choose the rule you’d will to be universal. “Press blue in this game” universalized saves everyone; “press red” universalized kills almost everyone. If you act by maxims you’d want everyone to follow in symmetric dilemmas, you pick blue.

- Altruistic expected value: Even if choices were independent, there’s a small chance your vote is pivotal; in that case, pressing blue saves nearly everyone. With N players and roughly balanced uncertainty, the probability of being pivotal scales about 1/√N, while the benefit if pivotal is O(N) lives saved. Expected lives saved therefore grows like √N—often easily swamping your personal survival risk if you give any appreciable weight to others’ lives.

- Equilibrium selection via norms/commitment: Societies that cultivate the norm “press blue in this scenario” select the payoff-dominant equilibrium and avoid catastrophic coordination failures. Being the type who presses blue improves long-run collective outcomes (reputation, culture, future repeats, acausal cooperation) even if any single round is private.

- Practical belief-updating: If you think there’s a decent chance that a blue majority will form (because many people are prosocial or reason superrationally), then pressing blue is close to costless to you and slightly increases the chance of the good equilibrium by aligning with that expectation.

Bottom line
- If you only value your own survival and treat your choice as causally independent of others’, red is the individually rational move.
- If you use superrational/evidential reasoning, care about social welfare, or want to help the world land on the payoff-dominant equilibrium, blue has a powerful case. In symmetric problems where what “your kind of agent” does is mirrored by many others, pressing blue is the policy that saves everyone—including, in expectation, you.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short answer: You’d see a split. The button people press tracks their goals, beliefs about others, and the decision theory they implicitly use—not their demographics per se. Here’s who, realistically, tends to end up on each side.

More likely to press red
- Narrow self-interest under causal reasoning: People who reason “my action doesn’t cause others’,” and look for weakly dominant moves. This includes many trained in classical game theory or economics who’ve internalized “take the dominant strategy.”
- “Anti-sucker” preference and pessimism about coordination: People who strongly dislike being the one who dies when others go red; people with low generalized trust or who expect fragmentation.
- Personal risk focus: Those who weight their own survival far above others’, or who are highly loss-averse for personal outcomes.
- Primed for dominance: Participants who’ve just been taught about dominance/iterated deletion, or who face high stakes and ample time to calculate.
Empirical anchor: In social-dilemma labs, subjects with economics/game-theory training defect more and contribute less to public goods (e.g., Marwell & Ames 1981; Frank, Gilovich & Regan 1993).

More likely to press blue
- Prosocial/value-universalist types: People high on Social Value Orientation (prosocial), rule utilitarians/Kantians who ask “what rule should everyone follow?” and pick the payoff-dominant norm.
- Superrational/correlated-reasoners: Folks who buy Hofstadter/Parfit-style arguments, updateless/evidential decision theories, or acausal cooperation: “If I’m the kind of person who presses blue, many similar others are too; that’s the world where everyone lives.”
- Expected-value altruists: People who give real weight to others’ lives and note that a small “pivotal” chance times a huge benefit (saving billions) yields enormous expected social value.
- Identity and norm builders: People motivated to be the type who cooperates in symmetric dilemmas, to sustain norms for future repeats and related problems.
- Optimists about coordination/high-trust: Those who think a blue majority is plausible already and want to align with it.
Empirical anchor: In one-shot social dilemmas, large minorities (often 30–60%) cooperate even when defection is individually dominant; cooperation rises with trust and prosocial orientation, and under time pressure for people with cooperative priors (e.g., Rand et al. 2012).

Situational factors that shift the split
- Framing: Emphasizing “red weakly dominates” pushes red; emphasizing “blue majority saves everyone” pushes blue.
- Stakes and time: Higher personal stakes and more deliberation push red; quick, intuitive responses among generally prosocial people push blue.
- Beliefs about others: Expecting many similar reasoners (or having public commitments/norms) pushes blue; expecting heterogeneity or cynicism pushes red.
- Community norms: Rationalist/EA-style circles that endorse superrational policies will skew blue; standard econ/game-theory classrooms skew red.

Bottom line
- In a mass, anonymous, one-shot setting that highlights dominance, expect a red majority.
- In communities with strong cooperative norms, high trust, or superrational commitments—and when the prompt frames the universalizable rule—expect many to press blue, sometimes enough to win.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. Pressing blue is irrational only under a narrow set of assumptions; under several common and coherent views it’s exactly the rational move.

When blue is (instrumentally) irrational
- Assumptions: you only care about your own survival; you use causal decision theory; you treat your action as independent of others’.
- Result: Red weakly dominates blue. There are possible worlds where red saves you and blue kills you, and none where blue saves you and red kills you. On that model, choosing blue is instrumentally irrational.

When blue is rational
- Altruistic or rule-based preferences: If you give any substantial weight to others’ lives or follow “the rule I’d will everyone to follow,” blue maximizes expected value. The pivotal case is rare but, multiplied by billions of lives, dominates the calculus.
- Correlated/superrational reasoning (EDT/FDT/Hofstadter): If you think many others reason like you, your choice is evidence about theirs. Adopting the policy “press blue in this setup” steers you into the world where most similar agents also press blue; that policy maximizes your survival in expectation and maximizes welfare.
- Cultural/long-run rationality: Being the type who presses blue helps select the payoff-dominant norm in your community and in future repeats of structurally similar dilemmas; that can be the prudent policy even if this round is private.
- Extreme beliefs: If you’re essentially certain a blue majority will form anyway, blue and red are outcome-equivalent for you; pressing blue isn’t irrational.

Bottom line
- Under narrow, self-interested, causal-independence assumptions, blue is instrumentally irrational.
- Under altruistic values, superrational/correlated decision theories, or norm-building objectives, pressing blue is a rational—and often the best—policy.
